language_wrapper: Consider a finite set S of distinct positive integers whose smallest element is 1 and whose largest element is {max_val}. It has the property that for every subset T of S with 1 ≤ |T| ≤ {d}, the arithmetic mean of the set obtained by deleting T (i.e., of S \ T) is an integer. Under these conditions, what is the greatest possible size of S?
hardness_rationale: The seed problem requires integrality of the mean after deleting a single element, which forces all elements to lie in a single residue class modulo n−1 and leads to a quadratic divisibility constraint. Our augmentation demands integrality for deletions of up to d elements (with d ≥ 2), which forces all elements simultaneously to lie in a single residue class modulo each of n−1, n−2, ..., n−d and therefore modulo their lcm. The resulting constraints couple a divisibility condition L(n, d) | (max_val − 1) with a cardinality condition (max_val − 1)/L(n, d) ≥ n − 1. For d = 2 this produces a cubic-type bound; for d = 3 it becomes quartic-scale, significantly more restrictive and algebraically intricate. Optimizing n under these joint conditions eliminates the possibility of guessing and requires a deeper structural understanding of congruences under multiple deletion regimes.
notes: Proof outline of correctness for the family: Let S be a set of size n with smallest element 1 and largest element M, and suppose that for each r ∈ {1, 2, ..., d} and every subset T ⊆ S with |T| = r, the mean of S \ T is an integer. Write s = sum(S). The hypothesis reads: for all T with |T| = r, s − sum(T) is divisible by n − r. Fix any r ∈ {1, ..., d} and fix r − 1 specific elements u1, ..., u_{r−1} ∈ S. For any y, z ∈ S distinct from those fixed, we have s − (u1 + ... + u_{r−1} + y) ≡ 0 (mod n − r) and s − (u1 + ... + u_{r−1} + z) ≡ 0 (mod n − r), so subtracting gives y ≡ z (mod n − r). Hence all elements of S are congruent modulo n − r. Since this holds for every r ≤ d, all elements lie in a single residue class modulo L := lcm(n − 1, n − 2, ..., n − d). Because 1 ∈ S and M ∈ S, we must have M ≡ 1 (mod L), i.e., L | (M − 1). The available candidates for S thus lie in the arithmetic progression A := {x ∈ [1, M] : x ≡ 1 (mod L)}, whose size is |A| = (M − 1)/L + 1. Any S must be a subset of A, so n ≤ |A|. Conversely, if L | (M − 1) and |A| ≥ n, then choose any n elements of A that include both 1 and M (possible iff (M − 1)/L ≥ n − 1), and for any T with |T| = r ≤ d, each element of S is 1 modulo n − r, so sum(S) ≡ n (mod n − r) and sum(T) ≡ r (mod n − r), implying sum(S) − sum(T) ≡ n − r ≡ 0 (mod n − r). Thus the mean of S \ T is integral for all r ≤ d, establishing sufficiency. Therefore the greatest possible size of S is the maximum n ≥ d + 1 satisfying L(n, d) | (M − 1) and (M − 1)/L(n, d) + 1 ≥ n, where L(n, d) = lcm(n − 1, ..., n − d). The verifier computes this maximum directly. This generalization strictly contains the seed (the case d = 1) and becomes substantially harder for d ≥ 2 due to the interaction of multiple congruence conditions and the growth of the lcm.
source_question: A set $\mathcal{S}$ of distinct positive integers has the following property: for every integer $x$ in $\mathcal{S},$ the arithmetic mean of the set of values obtained by deleting $x$ from $\mathcal{S}$ is an integer.  Given that 1 belongs to $\mathcal{S}$ and that 2002 is the largest element of $\mathcal{S},$ what is the greatest number of elements that $\mathcal{S}$ can have?
